It sets itself apart from basic texture-based MIP by storing only necessary voxels and from level-by-level MMIP by offering finer granularity in approximation error control [S1].

The claim states that the method sets itself apart from basic texture-based MIP by 'storing only necessary voxels'. The evidence supports that the method stores attributes (level and intensity) and uses a histogram to select coefficients, but it does not explicitly state that it stores 'only necessary voxels' as a defining distinction from basic texture-based MIP in the provided text. More importantly, the claim states it sets itself apart from level-by-level MMIP by 'offering finer granularity in approximation error control'. The evidence states that the error-sorted list is used to 'guide the error for speed/quality tradeoff' and that a percentage of coefficients is chosen. While this implies control over approximation, the text does not explicitly claim 'finer granularity' compared to level-by-level MMIP. In fact, level-by-level MMIP renders levels separately, which might offer different granularity. The text focuses on efficiency (avoiding point sprites, reducing memory to 4 bytes) rather than superior granularity of error control as the primary differentiator. Therefore, while some aspects of the implementation are supported, the specific comparative claims about 'storing only necessary voxels' and 'finer granularity' are not fully supported or are misinterpreted from the text.

This variant avoids the drawbacks of the basic implementation (point sprites, frame buffer blending, 6-byte overhead) by using a histogram-based selection strategy [S1].

The claim states that the variant avoids the drawbacks of the basic implementation (point sprites, frame buffer blending, 6-byte overhead) by using a histogram-based selection strategy. Source [S1] explicitly states in Section 4.6 ('Optimized streaming MIP') that the method uses a 'second histogram-sorting step' and that 'This results in a more efficient method for streaming MIP that avoids using point sprites and frame buffer blending, and which uses only four bytes per voxel.' Furthermore, Section 4.5 identifies the basic implementation's drawbacks as requiring 6 bytes per voxel, using point sprites, and requiring frame buffer blending (maximum operator). Section 4.6 concludes that the new algorithm has 'all the advantages of streaming MIP without any of the drawbacks mentioned in section 4.5.' Thus, every fact in the claim is supported by the evidence.
